t: Distant Barcodes — Rearranging So No Two Adjacent Are Equal
o: We must permute the barcode array so that no two equal values sit next to each other. In example 1, `[1,1,1,2,2,2]` becomes `[2,1,2,1,2,1]` by alternating the two values. In example 2, four 1s are spread across even indices (0,2,4,6), then remaining values fill odd and later even slots. Constraints ($n \le 10^4$, values $\le 10^4$) mean an answer is guaranteed to exist — the most frequent value appears at most $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ times — so a counting-based greedy or heap approach easily fits in time.
k: The most frequent value can appear at most ceil(n/2) times; placing it first at every other index guarantees it never self-adjacent.
Filling positions 0,2,4,... then 1,3,5,... with values sorted by frequency ensures any two copies of the same value are at least 2 apart.
A max-heap greedy (always place the most abundant remaining value) also works but is slower than direct even/odd placement.

a.i: At each step, greedily place the value with the largest remaining count, as long as it differs from the previously placed value. If it matches, use the second-most frequent instead. This works because always consuming the scarcest-safe option keeps counts balanced; since the max count never exceeds the sum of others plus one, we never get stuck.
s: Count occurrences of each value with a hash map.
Push (count, value) pairs into a max-heap.
Repeatedly pop the top; if it equals the last placed value, pop the second instead and push the first back.
Append the chosen value, decrement its count, and push it back if count > 0.
a.t: O(n log k) where k is the number of distinct values (k <= n); each of n placements does O(log k) heap work.
a.sp: O(k) for the counter and heap plus O(n) for the output.

a.i: Sort distinct values by descending frequency and write them into positions 0, 2, 4, ... wrapping to 1, 3, 5, .... Since the most frequent value occupies every other slot starting at index 0, its copies are separated by exactly one other element; all subsequent values have smaller counts, so they too fit without adjacency conflicts. This avoids any heap or comparison sort over elements.
s: Count frequencies; bucket values by count into an array indexed by count (counts <= n).
Iterate counts from high to low, collecting values.
Maintain a position pointer starting at 0, jumping by 2; when it exceeds n-1, reset to 1.
For each value, write it `count` times at successive positions.
a.t: O(n + V) time — counting is O(n), bucket iteration touches each element once; V = 10001 constant bound on values.
a.sp: O(n + V) for buckets, counter, and output array.

w: In an interview, lead with the heap greedy to show reasoning, then present the even/odd counting solution as the optimal linear-time refinement. Pitfalls: forgetting to reset the pointer from even to odd indices when wrapping; assuming sorting the raw array suffices (it doesn't — equal values cluster); edge cases include n = 1 (return as-is) and a single repeated value like [7,7,7] which is impossible per constraints' guarantee but worth mentioning. Follow-ups: generalize to 'no k adjacent equal', rearrange a string similarly (LeetCode 767), or handle streaming input where you can't see all data upfront.
